author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Shore I Keep Choosing
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The loose board was still loose.

It was the same board beside our kitchen door that I'd noticed weeks ago and decided could wait until we finished the bridge inspection, then the drainage survey, then the festival, then the endless sequence of ordinary emergencies that made a life.

Now the whole village had gathered for a small celebration, and Maui was standing on the porch staring at the board like it was an ancient enemy.

"We could fix that," he said.

"We could."

"Right now?"

I looked past him toward the sea. Tideglass Cove glittered in late afternoon light. The sea-glass orchard had grown slowly across three modest beds, the original wild flowers still holding the dunes in place. The upper route had fresh lanterns, and the temporary surface channel carried runoff away from the lower houses. Beneath the arch, the old maintenance passage remained sealed, its history not yet fully understood.

People would still have work to do tomorrow.

"Yes," I said. "Right now."

We fetched the tools.

The board had lifted because one fastener had worked loose after repeated changes in humidity. Nothing dramatic. No curse. No ancient enemy beneath the wood.

Maui held it steady while I measured the replacement. We checked that the new fastener was rated for coastal conditions. I drilled a pilot hole. He tightened the screw carefully enough not to split the timber.

Then we stepped back.

The board held.

"Magnificent," he said.

I laughed.

"I know."

He looked at me with an expression so warm it made my chest ache.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

He kissed me right there beside the repaired board, in the smell of sawdust and salt air. His hands settled gently at my waist. I caught his collar and drew him closer, forgetting for a moment that the village was waiting for us at the square.

A voice called from the path.

"If you two are finished fighting the porch, we're starting without you!"

Toph.

Maui leaned his forehead against mine.

"She's very difficult."

"She likes you."

"Tragic."

We laughed and went to the celebration.

It wasn't a grand finale. There were no fireworks, no battle, no prophecy fulfilled. The festival committee had planned a supper and a small Lantern Walk to thank the people who'd maintained the safe routes through a difficult season.

Mara had brought bread. Iroh poured tea from the affordable house blend. Danse and Renn were showing a curious visitor how to repair a simple hinge. Greg was tuning his guitar beside the western bench. Severus stood near Moonroot's display table, speaking with Orin about a newly cataloged maintenance receipt.

Aang helped children hang paper kites where they wouldn't block the path. Katara checked the water station before sitting down to eat. Toph complained that the lantern poles were crooked and then adjusted them without being asked to give a speech.

I loved them.

All of them, in different ways, for different reasons.

None of those relationships had become a secret or a mistake because this chapter of my life with Maui was reaching a quiet place.

He looked around the square.

"You have a very crowded life," he said.

"Yes."

"Does it ever frighten you?"

"Sometimes."

He nodded.

"Me too."

We sat on the low stone wall beside the fountain. The air smelled of bread and wet leaves. A child was trying to explain a game involving six paper fish to a very confused Danse.

I watched the scene for a while, smiling.

"When I first arrived," I said, "I thought finding a home meant finding the one place where I was supposed to stay."

"And now?"

"Now I think home is where I can tell the truth, leave when I need to, and come back because I want to."

Maui looked at me.

"Even when you love other people?"

"Especially then. I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. That hasn't changed. But neither has the fact that I love you."

He took my hand.

"I know."

I searched his face.

"Do you?"

He smiled.

"I know enough to keep asking the real questions."

I laughed softly.

"That's fair."

We sat together while the first lanterns were lit.

Near the notice board, Tomas was speaking with Neri about his departure in a few days. He had chosen to return for a visit, and he would choose when to leave again. Vel was selling baskets without being asked to explain how she felt about him. Mereana's visiting group had sent a note confirming the new artwork lending agreement, with their next visit scheduled only when they wished to return.

The valley was full of people who were not waiting for me to give them endings.

That was one of the things I loved most about it.

The supper began.

Greg played his new song, the one with the space between the notes. Iroh smiled as he listened. Toph tapped the rhythm through the stone with the heel of her boot, and Aang laughed when a paper fish landed on his shoulder.

Maui did not tell a heroic story.

He passed bread to the child beside him, then asked whether they wanted the last piece. The child said no.

He put it back.

I nearly cried at the simplicity of it.

Later, as the square grew quiet, we walked toward Tideglass by the upper route. The lanterns were bright enough to guide us, but not so bright they hid the stars. The sea moved beyond the garden, steady and indifferent to the little dramas of our lives.

At the signal post, I stopped.

"Can I tell you what I want?" I asked.

Maui turned toward me.

"Always."

"I want to keep choosing you. Not as a reward for the things you've done. Not because I'm afraid of being alone. Because I like the person who argues about laundry, carries blankets, learns to apologize, and makes terrible fish carvings."

He looked down, smiling.

"I want to keep choosing you too," he said. "Not because you stay only with me. Because you tell me the truth. Because you ask what I need. Because you laugh when I'm ridiculous and still believe I can learn."

I took his hand.

"Those are current promises," I said.

"Not forever?"

"Forever is too easy to say when the hard part is tomorrow."

He considered that.

"Then tomorrow," he said.

"Tomorrow."

He kissed me softly beneath the lanterns. The sea breeze moved through my hair, and the garden smelled of rosemary. I thought of the green notebook waiting at home, full of questions I'd learned to ask and answers that had changed as I did.

We stayed until the last visitors had gone.

Then we walked down the path toward our kitchen door.

The repaired board held beneath our feet.

Inside, the little wooden fish watched from the shelf. The calendar hung beside the stove. Our living agreement rested in the green notebook, with space left at the bottom for revisions neither of us could predict.

Maui set down the lantern.

"Do you want tea?"

"Yes."

"Do you want me to make it?"

I looked at him.

"How much cinnamon were you planning to add?"

He grinned.

"An heroic amount."

"Then I'll supervise."

We made tea together.

Outside, the Threadway remained open. There would be other visits, other loves, other repairs, and questions we hadn't yet learned how to ask. The old service passage still waited beneath the stone, not as a promise that every mystery must be solved tonight, but as a responsibility the community would continue to examine.

I didn't need the whole world to stand still for my happiness to be real.

Maui handed me a cup.

I took it.

And when he asked whether I wanted to stay a little longer, I smiled and answered the only way that mattered.

"Yes. Tonight, I do."
